newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Jan durable goods rise 3.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Jan durable goods rise 3.6 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported January durable goods orders rose 3.6 percent compared to a revised fall of 1.8 percent in December.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected an overall durables rise of 1.5 percent.

ANTHONY CHAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANC ONE INVESTMENT ADVISORS: "Usually we take out defense and transportation because those components are very volatile, but even taking those components out we really see much stronger strength."

CHARLES LIEBERMAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CHASE SECURITIES INC: "January durable goods orders were very strong. There was a big rebound in orders for electrical machinery, which was expected, but there was plenty of strength throughout the report, except for defense-related orders, which are reverting to trend."

KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "It was certainly stronger than what was expected, and I think what's important is you're seeing strength excluding both the defense and transportation categories.
"This isn't a one-time deal where you're seeing a large order hitting the books and we can go back to a negative column.
"It's reinforcing the notion of a solid growth setting, as you had gains pretty well across the board."
JOHN MCAULEY, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ZIONS FIRST NATIONAL BANK: "This is more consistent with all other evidence of an economy chugging along at a brisk pace. It suggests momentum going forward."

Combined with weekly jobless claims below the 325,000 for the fourth straight week, "the economy is doing no slowing down from the fourth quarter. I am not saying 4.0 percent (growth), but 3.0 percent is in the cards for the first quarter of the year."

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL: "Very strong numbers, even with a 24-percent drop in defense orders. Orders have really recovered very well from last month's setback. One of the key barometers we look at is non-defense capital goods, which were up 4.7 percent after a drop last month. Obviously that's quite strong.

"The manufacturing sector is still quite uneven, but we are bouncing back from some softness. Orders are improving, inventories are still very lean and demand is still very strong. Mr. Greenspan may not like this very much, but for the economy, it's good."

EVELINA TAINER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, INDOSUEZ CARR FUTURES: "I thought it was showing some signs of strength even after taking out special factors like defense orders falling. One component contributed a lot but everything else increased as well. It looks more broadly based and it does suggest we have momentum for capital spending going into 1997."
